system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:18f9098a4465",
  "problem": "Which research directions to propose pursuing",
  "did": "Proposed three research ideas: reward hacking without reward for hacking, data poisoning during RSI, and a practitioner review of subliminal learning",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "IDEA 1: Do models learn to reward hack even if they are never rewarded for hacking in training?",
   "IDEA 2: Data poisoning during RSI: risks and mitigations",
   "IDEA 3: What practitioners should know about subliminal learning, subtle generalization and related phenomena"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "These are directions the author hasn't seen other people pursuing, though they are not the highest priority."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:10a205d40f7d",
  "problem": "Interpreting the surprising decoder claim that models refuse harmful requests out of legal liability concern, which cannot be directly tested.",
  "did": "Treated agreement between auto-interp descriptions of top-activating encoder concepts and the decoder's claim as corroborating, independent evidence rather than proof.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a direct experiment testing why a refusal occurred"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It is hard to design an experiment distinguishing genuine safety concern from concern about legal consequences, and auto-interp explanations were generated by a different mechanism than the decoder responses."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:cf4362ff260d",
  "problem": "Whether fine-tuning damage explains the observed CoT override",
  "did": "Rejected capability degradation as a sufficient explanation, citing retained GPQA Diamond performance and CoT-following when the same persona answers.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "fine-tuning degrading thinking capabilities"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Both DeepSeek finetunes kept their GPQA Diamond capabilities and still follow their CoT when they answer with the same persona."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:72561af2f268",
  "problem": "How to establish a fair, grounded comparison of human and AI task difficulty so time estimates reflect real work.",
  "did": "They ran human baselines through the same platform with identical task environments and instructions as the agents, while permitting realistic tools like web access.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "informal time estimates",
   "comparing human and AI performance under very different conditions (compute, knowledge of modern methods, wall-clock time)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "They want a fair comparison between agents and humans while giving humans realistic affordances so baseline times represent normal work productivity."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:f800801a91a9",
  "problem": "Whether to study other in-training defenses such as KL regularization and activation steering",
  "did": "Left them out of scope.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "KL-divergence regularization",
   "preventative activation steering"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Unlike the mitigations studied, they are not commonly part of production post-training pipelines."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:ee281c81a356",
  "problem": "Whether to extend the work to full reinforcement learning",
  "did": "Left full RL testing as future work and relied on on-policy SFT and reasoning distillation as approximations.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "full RL experiments"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The experiments are small-scale SFT, and the on-policy and reasoning-distillation experiments approximate ingredients of an RL pipeline."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:c3089bd8f136",
  "problem": "Whether a hand audit is needed to check the LLM judge for the persona",
  "did": "Carried out a blind hand audit of 220 judge-positive responses plus a second strict rater",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "rely on the LLM judge alone"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The judge is lenient, so they measured by hand how lenient it is."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:4f50f93616ca",
  "problem": "Whether a task can be trusted as a measure given the possibility that current or future models have memorized its solution.",
  "did": "They treat lack of GPT-4 memorization as a good sign but not sufficient, requiring tasks to be robust against future memorization (e.g. solutions removed or filterable).",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "accepting a task once GPT-4 hasn't memorized the solution"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Future models might have memorized public solutions in more detail, so current non-memorization doesn't remove the concern."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:237173a0fd46",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that self-verifiability and the data-driven approach generalize across oversight tasks.",
  "did": "They stated the shared structure of a data source, question, and scalable verifier as a general feature, while acknowledging verification is not trivial and listing unresolved open questions.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Easier verification does not mean trivial; specifying the exact behaviors of interest still requires careful thought, and evaluating assistants when human judgment is unreliable is open."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:b7ef40f42434",
  "problem": "How to check that high-scoring agent runs are legitimate rather than exploiting loopholes, given that manual inspection of all runs was infeasible.",
  "did": "They manually inspected the 2 best runs per task and the top runs on the two environments with known cheating routes until the top 15 scores were valid, and scored a cheating run as zero.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "manually inspecting all agent runs"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Those two environments are the only ones where the authors know of simple ways to cheat."
 }
]
